course.title: Deterministic Concurrency
course.description: Concurrency bugs are the ones that pass every test on your laptop and corrupt a balance in production once a week. They depend on timing: which thread ran between someone else's read and write. A test that starts threads and hopes to hit the bad timing is a test that passes by luck. This module teaches the ideas (lost updates, atomics, immutable snapshots, executors, futures, queues, deadlocks) **and** the habit that makes concurrent code testable: separate the logic from the scheduling, then drive the scheduling yourself. Every test here gives the same answer on every run and finishes well under a second.

lessons.title: Deterministic Concurrency
lessons.explanation:
# 17 · Deterministic Concurrency

Concurrency bugs are the ones that pass every test on your laptop and
corrupt a balance in production once a week. They depend on timing:
which thread ran between someone else's read and write. A test that
starts threads and hopes to hit the bad timing is a test that passes by
luck. This module teaches the ideas (lost updates, atomics, immutable
snapshots, executors, futures, queues, deadlocks) **and** the habit
that makes concurrent code testable: separate the logic from the
scheduling, then drive the scheduling yourself. Every test here gives
the same answer on every run and finishes well under a second.

## The mental model

### 1 · A race is an interleaving you did not plan for

```
counter = 0        A: read 0          B: read 0
                   A: write 1         B: write 1      → counter = 1, one increment lost
```

`counter++` is read, add, write. Any step of another thread can land
between them. With two workers doing two increments each there are 70
interleavings, and only 6 give the right answer (exercise 01 counts
them). That is why "it passed 50 times" proves nothing.

### 2 · Three ways to be safe, from simplest to hardest

| approach | how | used for | exercises |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| don't share mutable state | immutable snapshots, swap one reference | config, prices, routing tables | 03 |
| make each update one atomic step | `AtomicInteger`, `LongAdder`, CAS loops, `ConcurrentHashMap.merge/compute` | counters, stock, caches | 01, 02, 04 |
| hand work between threads through a safe channel | executors, `CompletableFuture`, `BlockingQueue` | pipelines, fan-out/fan-in | 05, 06, 07 |
| locks | `synchronized`, `ReentrantLock`, always in one global order | multi-object invariants | 08 |

Prefer the higher rows. Every lock you add is a lock that can be taken
in the wrong order.

### 3 · Compare-and-set is the primitive under the atomics

```java
while (true) {
    int now = left.get();
    if (now == 0) return false;                     // the condition
    if (left.compareAndSet(now, now - 1)) return true;  // only if nobody moved first
}                                                   // someone did: re-read, retry
```

`updateAndGet` and `accumulateAndGet` are this loop, written for you
(`incrementAndGet` too, in effect), and the function you pass may run
more than once, so it must have no side effects.
`ConcurrentHashMap.compute`, `merge` and `computeIfAbsent` work
differently: they lock that key's bin and run the function once, so
keep the function short and never touch the same map from inside it.

### 4 · Make the scheduler a parameter

```
production:  new EmailBatcher(Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8), smtp)
test:        new EmailBatcher(manualExecutor, fakeMailer)   // nothing runs until runAll()
test:        new EmailBatcher(Runnable::run, fakeMailer)    // everything runs inline
```

The same goes for futures (complete them by hand in the test), for
time (inject a `Clock`, module 04 and the system-design block), and for
the interleaving itself: replay a schedule string (exercises 01 and 07),
or hand the code a rival that acts between its read and its write
(exercises 02 to 04), so a race fails on every run, not once a week.
Real threads appear in a few tests here only where the RESULT is
independent of the order: exact totals, FIFO output from a single
consumer, results collected by index.

## The details that bite

1. **Read-modify-write is not atomic.** `x++`, `map.put(k, map.get(k) + 1)`
   and `if (get() > 0) decrement()` all lose updates (exercises 01, 02, 04).
2. **A failed CAS must re-read.** Retrying from the stale value makes
   the same mistake again (exercise 01).
3. **`getAndDecrement() > 0` answers right and leaves the count
   negative** (exercise 02).
4. **"Keep the max" is a read-modify-write too.** Use
   `accumulateAndGet(v, Math::max)` (exercise 02).
5. **`Map.copyOf` of a map of lists shares the lists.** Immutable means
   all the way down (exercise 03).
6. **`getAndUpdate` returns the OLD value; `updateAndGet` the new**
   (exercise 03).
7. **A remapping function returning `null` removes the key;**
   `computeIfPresent` never creates one (exercise 04).
8. **`computeIfAbsent` does not cache `null`** (exercise 04).
9. **A test executor must be FIFO, survive failing tasks and refuse to
   spin forever** (exercise 05).
10. **`Future.get` wraps the task's exception; report `getCause()`**
    (exercises 05, 06).
11. **`allOf` is not fail-fast, and `anyOf` is not first-success**
    (exercise 06).
12. **A producer whose offer failed must keep the item,** and an idle
    producer is not waiting (exercise 07).
13. **Stop a consumer with a poison pill that cannot be real data**
    (exercise 07).
14. **Only locks still held create ordering edges, and reentrant
    acquisition is not a self-deadlock** (exercise 08).

## Cheat table

| want | write |
| --- | --- |
| count from many threads | `LongAdder.increment()`, read with `sum()` |
| conditional atomic update | CAS loop on `AtomicInteger`, or `updateAndGet` with a pure function |
| add to a map entry | `map.merge(k, n, Integer::sum)` |
| update-or-remove a map entry | `map.computeIfPresent(k, (k, v) -> ... null to remove)` |
| load once per key | `map.computeIfAbsent(k, loader)` |
| publish a new immutable snapshot | `AtomicReference.updateAndGet(old -> old.withX(...))` |
| join two async results | `a.thenCombine(b, (x, y) -> ...)` |
| failure as a default value | `f.exceptionally(e -> fallback)` |
| bounded hand-off between threads | `ArrayBlockingQueue.put` / `take` + a poison pill |
| never deadlock on two locks | acquire in one global order (sorted ids) |

## Exercises

| # | file | ★ | what you build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | `01-lost-updates.java` | ★☆☆ | replayable interleavings: lost updates, CAS retries, outcome counts |
| 02 | `02-atomic-counters.java` | ★☆☆ | lock-free request metrics and a ticket pool with CAS loops |
| 03 | `03-immutable-snapshots.java` | ★☆☆ | a deeply immutable config published through an `AtomicReference` |
| 04 | `04-concurrent-map-ops.java` | ★★☆ | stock reservations with `merge`/`computeIfPresent`, a `computeIfAbsent` loader |
| 05 | `05-manual-executor.java` | ★★☆ | a test executor you step by hand, and code that takes an `Executor` |
| 06 | `06-completable-futures.java` | ★★☆ | quote, fail-fast all, first-success and a deadline, completed by hand |
| 07 | `07-producer-consumer.java` | ★★☆ | a steppable bounded-buffer model, then a real `BlockingQueue` pipeline |
| 08 | `08-deadlock-detector.java` | ★★★ | lock-order graphs from traces, cycle finding, and a safe global lock order |

Do the warm-ups and core in order. Stretch if time allows. Exercise 04
is module 09's single-flight cache loader in one line, 07 is module 12's
bounded queue with real threads, and 08's "lock in one global order" is
the standard fix for the transfer deadlock between two bank accounts.

---

**Next:** `bootcamp/18-parsing-and-serialization`

javabootcamp/17-deterministic-concurrenc.instructions:
**Concepts:** race conditions · read-modify-write · interleavings · CAS  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

counter++ is two steps: READ the counter into a register, then WRITE
register + 1. Replay it by hand: in a schedule like "ABAB" each letter
is a worker (capital letters only, else IllegalArgumentException)
taking its next step, and each worker alternates READ, WRITE, READ...

  runPlain(s)     the final counter with plain writes
  lostUpdates(s)  completed writes minus the final counter (plain)
  runCas(s)       CasRun(counter, failedWrites): a WRITE is a
                  compare-and-set that only succeeds if the counter
                  still holds the value READ; a failed WRITE is
                  counted and that worker's next step is a READ again
  outcomes(n)     for two workers doing n increments each (4n steps),
                  how often each final value occurs over EVERY
                  interleaving, as a sorted map

    runPlain("AABB") → 2   runPlain("ABAB") → 1   outcomes(1) → {1=4, 2=2}

hint: a worker that has read but not yet written holds a register.
javabootcamp/17-deterministic-concurrenc.explanation:
Every concurrency bug in this module starts here. counter++ compiles to
a read, an add and a write, and the scheduler may run another thread
between them. "ABAB" is the lost update: both read 0, both write 1,
one increment vanishes. A test that runs real threads hits this only
sometimes, which is why this exercise replays the interleavings by hand
instead: the same schedule always gives the same answer.
outcomes(n) makes the scale of the problem concrete. With one increment
each, 4 of the 6 interleavings lose an update. With two each, only 6 of
70 give the right answer of 4. Real threads usually run each worker's
steps back to back, so a threaded test mostly passes anyway.
COMPARE-AND-SET is how AtomicInteger fixes it without a lock. The write
says "set to r + 1 only if the value is still r". When another worker
got there first, the CAS fails, nothing is overwritten, and the worker
reads again and retries. updateAndGet() is exactly that retry loop;
incrementAndGet() means the same, though the JIT may use one atomic
add instruction (LOCK XADD on x86). Under CAS no completed increment
is ever lost; contention costs retries instead.
The register map is the detail: a worker with a pending READ holds a
stale copy, and the bug is writing from it.

javabootcamp/17-deterministic-concurrenc.instructions:
**Concepts:** AtomicInteger · AtomicLong · LongAdder · compare-and-set loops  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A web server's request metrics and a concert's ticket pool, both safe
to call from many threads without a lock. Finish:
  Metrics.record(ms)  count one request and add its ms (ms < 0 →
                      IllegalArgumentException, nothing recorded);
                      requests(), totalMillis(), slowest() (0 before
                      any request), averageMillis() (0.0 before any)
  TicketPool(n)       n < 0 → IllegalArgumentException; keep the count
                      in Counter.atomic(n), an AtomicInteger
  tryTake()           take one ticket if any is left; the count never
                      goes below zero
  takeUpTo(n)         atomically take min(n, left) and return how many
                      were taken; n < 0 → IllegalArgumentException
  left()              tickets left
Some tests build the pool on the given RivalCounter, where a rival
takes a ticket right after your read, on every run. Two more run real
threads; correct code gives the exact totals every time.

    new TicketPool(1): tryTake() → true, tryTake() → false, left() → 0

hint: compareAndSet(expected, next) fails if someone else moved first.
javabootcamp/17-deterministic-concurrenc.explanation:
java.util.concurrent.atomic gives single variables that update without
a lock: incrementAndGet and addAndGet are read-modify-write in one
indivisible step. LongAdder is the better counter when many threads
write and few read: it spreads increments over cells and adds them up
in sum(), which is why metrics libraries use it.
"Keep the maximum" is a read-modify-write too: get() then set() can let
a smaller value overwrite a bigger one that arrived in between.
accumulateAndGet(ms, Math::max) runs the CAS retry loop for you.
The ticket pool needs a condition ("only if one is left"), and no
single atomic method says that, so you write the CAS loop yourself:
read, decide, compareAndSet(read, read - 1), retry if it failed. The
tempting `if (left.get() > 0) left.decrementAndGet()` is check-then-
act: two threads both see 1 and both decrement. getAndDecrement() > 0
is wrong a different way: it returns the right answer but leaves the
count negative.
The count sits behind a Counter so a test can play the rival thread:
RivalCounter takes a ticket right after your read, the moment a check-
then-act or a stale write breaks, so those bugs fail on EVERY run. The
threaded tests only show the totals; a racy max in slowest() can still
pass them by luck, which is why you check the design, not the luck.

javabootcamp/17-deterministic-concurrenc.instructions:
**Concepts:** immutability · defensive copies · AtomicReference · publication  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A router's configuration is read on every request and replaced now and
then. Make it safe by design: immutable snapshots, swapped atomically.
  Config(name, hosts, routes)  copies its inputs DEEPLY: later changes
                    to the caller's list, map or a route's list never
                    show up inside the Config
  hosts(), routes() read-only views: any change through them, even to
                    a route's list, throws UnsupportedOperationException
  withHost(h)       a new Config with h appended; this one is unchanged
  withRoute(p, ts)  a new Config with route p set to ts (copied)
  ConfigHolder      current() returns the published snapshot;
                    update(change) applies change to it atomically and
                    returns the NEW snapshot. If another update lands
                    while change runs, change runs AGAIN on the newer
                    snapshot. A reader keeps the snapshot it holds
One test runs 4 threads x 250 withHost updates: all 1,000 must arrive.

    holder.update(c -> c.withHost("h2"))  → the new Config, hosts [h1, h2]

hint: List.copyOf copies one level; a map of lists needs two.
javabootcamp/17-deterministic-concurrenc.explanation:
The simplest thread-safe object is one that never changes. An
immutable Config can be read by any number of threads with no locks,
and a reader can never see half an update, because there are no
updates: a change builds a NEW Config and swaps the reference. Final
class, private final fields, and deep copies on the way in and out.
Defensive copying is where it goes wrong. Storing the caller's list
lets them change your "immutable" object later. List.copyOf and
Map.copyOf make unmodifiable copies, but a Map<String, List<String>>
copied with Map.copyOf still shares the inner lists: copy each value.
SAFE PUBLICATION is the second half. A plain field written by one
thread may never become visible to another. AtomicReference (like a
volatile field) guarantees that a reader that sees the new reference
also sees the fully built object behind it, and final fields add the
same guarantee for the object's contents.
update uses updateAndGet, a CAS retry loop: if two threads update at
once, one retries its function on the newer snapshot, so no update is
lost. A test makes that happen on every run by updating from INSIDE a
change; get() then set() loses the rival's host. The retry only works
because the function is pure; one that charges money would run twice.
getAndUpdate returns the OLD snapshot, the classic slip.

javabootcamp/17-deterministic-concurrenc.instructions:
**Concepts:** ConcurrentHashMap · merge · computeIfPresent · computeIfAbsent  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A warehouse shared by many request threads. Every update must be ONE
atomic map call, never a get followed by a put. Finish:
  receive(sku, n)   add n to what is on hand (n < 1 →
                    IllegalArgumentException)
  reserve(sku, n)   take n only if at least n are on hand, and say
                    whether it did; taking the last unit REMOVES the
                    sku; an unknown sku → false and nothing is created;
                    n < 1 → IllegalArgumentException
  onHand(sku), skus()   current quantity (0 if absent), stocked skus
  Loader.get(key)   load through computeIfAbsent: the source runs once
                    per key; if it returns null nothing is cached, so
                    the next get tries again; loads() counts source calls
  wordCounts(lines) counts of each space-separated word, built from a
                    PARALLEL stream into a ConcurrentHashMap
Two tests hand Stock and Loader the given RivalMap, which runs a rival's
call right after your next get(): a get-then-put fails on every run.

    receive(bolt, 3); reserve(bolt, 5) → false; reserve(bolt, 3) → true

hint: a remapping function that returns null removes the entry.
javabootcamp/17-deterministic-concurrenc.explanation:
ConcurrentHashMap is safe for concurrent use, but only call by call.
`map.put(k, map.get(k) + n)` is two calls with a gap between them:
two threads both read 3, both write 4, and one delivery disappears.
The fix is to hand the map a FUNCTION and let it apply it atomically
for that key: merge(k, n, Integer::sum) for "add", and compute or
computeIfPresent for anything with a condition.
reserve shows the full power of the remapping function. It sees the
current value, may refuse (return the same value), may update, and may
return null to REMOVE the entry, all while no other thread can touch
that key. "Reserve only if enough" cannot be expressed with get/put
safely at all. computeIfPresent also gives "unknown sku" for free: the
function never runs, and nothing is created.
computeIfAbsent is the cache-loading idiom: the loader runs at most
once per key even when many threads ask at the same moment, and a null
result is not stored. Keep the function short and never touch the same
map from inside it; that can deadlock or throw.
The RivalMap tests run a rival's call inside your get(), the exact gap
a get-then-put leaves, so that bug fails on every run. wordCounts and
the 8-thread test use real threads and check only totals, which do
not depend on the order the threads ran in.

javabootcamp/17-deterministic-concurrenc.instructions:
**Concepts:** Executor injection · deterministic scheduling · ExecutorService  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Code that takes an Executor can be tested with one YOU drive. Finish:
  ManualExecutor   execute(task) queues it (null → NullPointerException)
                   and runs nothing; pending() counts queued tasks;
                   runNext() runs the oldest, false if none; a task's
                   RuntimeException is caught and its message added to
                   failures(); runAll() runs until the queue is empty,
                   including tasks queued meanwhile, and returns how
                   many ran; if 10,000 have run and more are still
                   queued → IllegalStateException
  EmailBatcher     sendAll(recipients) queues one task per recipient,
                   in order; a send that throws is queued ONCE more at
                   the back; failing again adds it to gaveUp()
  runInOrder(single, tasks)  run Callables on a given ExecutorService
                   and return each result in INPUT order, or
                   "error: <cause's message>" for a task that threw

    sendAll([ana, bo, cy]) with bo failing once → sent ana, cy, bo

hint: invokeAll returns the futures in the order of the tasks.
javabootcamp/17-deterministic-concurrenc.explanation:
The surest way to make concurrent code testable is to not create
threads in it. EmailBatcher receives an Executor instead of starting
threads, so production passes a thread pool and the test passes a
ManualExecutor: nothing runs until the test calls runNext() or
runAll(), and then it runs in a known order on the test's own thread.
No sleeps, no timeouts, no flakiness. Executor direct = Runnable::run
is the other extreme: run immediately, inline.
The details of the manual executor are exactly what makes it useful.
FIFO order (a deque used as a queue, not a stack). Tasks that schedule
tasks go to the back and still run within runAll. A failing task is
recorded, not thrown into the test that happened to call runAll, and
a runaway task that keeps rescheduling itself fails loudly instead of
hanging the test.
The retry in EmailBatcher is queued at the BACK, after the recipients
already waiting, which is how a real queue treats a retry. Running it
inline would hide that order.
runInOrder shows that a real ExecutorService can also be deterministic
in its RESULT: invokeAll returns futures in task order, whatever order
the work ran in. Future.get() wraps a task's exception in an
ExecutionException; report its getCause().

javabootcamp/17-deterministic-concurrenc.instructions:
**Concepts:** CompletableFuture · thenCombine · exceptionally · fan-in  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A checkout asks three services at once. Tests complete every future BY
HAND, in chosen orders, so nothing depends on timing. Finish:
  quote(price, tax, discount)  price * (1 + tax) - discount, scale 2
                     HALF_UP, once all three are done; a failed discount
                     counts as 0; a failed price or tax fails the quote
                     with that same cause
  allInOrder(fs)     all values in INPUT order once all succeed; fails
                     with the cause as soon as ANY input fails, without
                     waiting for the rest; an empty list → []
  firstSuccess(fs)   the first value to arrive; failures are skipped
                     until every input has failed, then it fails with
                     IllegalStateException "all failed" (also for [])
  withDeadline(work, deadline, fallback)  work's value, or fallback if
                     the deadline future completes first

    quote(19.99, 0.25, 1.00) → 23.99

hint: completeExceptionally on your own result future reports early.
javabootcamp/17-deterministic-concurrenc.explanation:
CompletableFuture is a value that will exist later, plus callbacks to
run when it does. When the test thread calls complete(...), every
dependent stage runs right there, on the test thread, in a fixed
order. That is the trick of this exercise: no executor, no sleep, no
timeout, and the same result every run. Production code passes in
real futures from HTTP clients; the logic is the same.
thenCombine joins two futures; exceptionally turns a failure into a
value, which is how "no discount service, no discount" stays a
business rule instead of an outage. A dependent stage that fails
because its input failed holds a CompletionException wrapping the
original cause; join() throws it, and getCause() is what you report.
allOf is NOT "fail fast": it completes only when every input has
completed, even if the first one failed a second ago. allInOrder
builds its own result future and completes it exceptionally on the
first failure. Collect values by INDEX, not in arrival order.
anyOf takes the first to complete, success or failure, so it cannot
express "first success". Counting failures with an AtomicInteger and
failing only on the last is the honest version. withDeadline models a
timeout without a clock: in production the deadline future comes from
orTimeout or a scheduler; here the test fires it.

javabootcamp/17-deterministic-concurrenc.instructions:
**Concepts:** bounded buffers · backpressure · BlockingQueue · poison pill  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

First a model you can step by hand, then the real thing. Finish:
  BoundedBuffer(cap)  cap < 1 → IllegalArgumentException; offer(x)
                      adds at the back or returns false when full;
                      poll() takes from the front, empty if none
  simulate(cap, items, schedule)  a producer offers 1, 2, ... items
                      through a BoundedBuffer. 'P': offer the next; if
                      the buffer is full that is a producer wait (the
                      item stays next); once every item is in, 'P' does
                      nothing. 'C' is a consumer step: poll; empty is a
                      consumer wait. Others → IllegalArgumentException
  pipeline(input, cap, work)  a producer thread puts every input in an
                      ArrayBlockingQueue(cap), then a poison pill; a
                      consumer thread applies work until the pill; both
                      joined; returns the outputs in input order.
                      Any int is real data, -1 and 0 included

    simulate(2, 3, "PPPCPCC") → SimResult([1, 2, 3], 1, 0)

hint: Optional.empty() makes a pill no real item can be confused with.
javabootcamp/17-deterministic-concurrenc.explanation:
Producer-consumer is the shape of every queue in a system: request
handlers feeding a worker pool, a log shipper, the message brokers of
module 12. The BOUNDED buffer is the important word. When consumers
fall behind, a full buffer makes producers wait (backpressure) instead
of eating memory until the process dies.
The model makes backpressure visible and repeatable. A schedule of P
and C steps is one possible interleaving of two threads, and counting
waits tells you who is the bottleneck: producer waits mean the
consumer is too slow, consumer waits mean it is idle. Note that a
producer whose offer failed keeps the item; dropping it would be a
lost message. A producer with nothing left does no work, so its steps
are not waits.
pipeline is the same idea with real threads. ArrayBlockingQueue.put
blocks while full and take blocks while empty, so no polling and no
sleep. Shutdown is the classic problem: the consumer cannot tell
"empty for now" from "finished". A POISON PILL, a special item put
last, says "no more". Optional.empty() as the pill cannot collide with
a real value, unlike a magic -1. With one consumer FIFO order is kept,
so the result is deterministic even with real threads; several
consumers need one pill each, and their output order is not fixed.

javabootcamp/17-deterministic-concurrenc.instructions:
**Concepts:** deadlock · lock ordering · cycle detection · topological sort  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

Find deadlocks without running a thread. Each thread's trace is a list
of ops: "+a" acquires lock a, "-a" releases it. Finish:
  lockOrderGraph(traces)  an edge held → acquired for every lock held
        when another is first acquired. Locks are reentrant: "+a" while
        holding a adds no edge and needs one more "-a". Every lock seen
        is a key (sorted map, sorted sets). Releasing a lock not held →
        IllegalStateException "<thread> releases <lock> it does not
        hold"; an op not shaped +name or -name → IllegalArgumentException
  findCycle(graph)  a cycle as its locks, starting from its smallest
        lock, without repeating it, or empty. Search from each lock in
        sorted order, neighbours in sorted order; report the first found
  safeOrder(graph)  every lock once, each edge's source before its
        target, smallest available lock first; on a cycle,
        IllegalStateException "deadlock possible: a -> b -> a"

    T1 [+a, +b], T2 [+b, +a] → {a=[b], b=[a]} → findCycle → [a, b]

hint: a cycle in "acquired while holding" is a possible deadlock.
javabootcamp/17-deterministic-concurrenc.explanation:
A deadlock needs a cycle: T1 holds a and waits for b while T2 holds b
and waits for a. It depends on timing, so tests that run threads find
it by luck, and the JVM's ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() only
sees one that has already happened. Lock-order checkers (Linux's
lockdep) use a GRAPH instead: "b acquired while holding a" is an edge
a -> b, and a cycle means some interleaving CAN deadlock.
The graph rules carry the subtlety. Only locks still HELD create
edges; a released lock no longer orders anything. Reentrant
re-acquisition must not add a self-edge (a -> a would be a fake
deadlock) and must be counted, so the lock stays held until the last
release. A release of a lock not held is a bug in the trace, reported
with the thread's name.
findCycle is depth-first search with an "on the current path" set: an
edge back into the path closes a cycle. Normalising it to start at its
smallest lock makes the answer stable wherever the search entered.
safeOrder is the cure: a topological sort (Kahn's algorithm, with a
TreeSet or PriorityQueue for the alphabetical tie-break). If every
thread takes locks in that one global order, no cycle can form; that
is why "always lock accounts by ascending id" fixes transfer deadlocks.
